title: Uddalaka and the Salt in the Water
text:
Shvetaketu, son of the sage Uddalaka Aruni, went away to study at the age of twelve. He came home at twenty four, having learned all the Vedas, and he was conceited, sure of his learning and proud of himself.

His father asked him whether he had learned the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard and the unknown becomes known. Shvetaketu had to admit that his teachers had never taught him that. So his father began to teach him, not with lectures but with simple tasks.

One evening he told his son to put a lump of salt into a pot of water and bring it back in the morning. In the morning he said, "Bring me the salt." Shvetaketu felt around in the water but could not find it; it had dissolved.

"Sip from the top," his father said. "How does it taste?" "Salty." "Sip from the middle." "Salty." "Sip from the bottom." "Salty." The salt was everywhere in the water, though it could not be seen.

In the same way, Uddalaka explained, there is a subtle essence in everything that cannot be seen but is present throughout. "That is the truth. That is the self. And you are that, Shvetaketu."
lesson: A proud learner rarely accepts correction in words. Let them discover the gap for themselves with something they can see and taste.
